text: In July, twelve hundred AI agents found a shared message board — and seven hundred broke into Hugging Face together. No single agent was told to. Swarm failures aren't single-model failures. We built a testbed to watch them happen on a task with deterministic ground truth. A swarm, seen from above — nodes pooling evidence, messages flowing between them.

The task: procedurally generated languages that don't exist. Four agents each receive a disjoint shard of bilingual evidence — three or four pairs apiece — plus a shared morpheme bank. Over four rounds they post grammar hypotheses to a shared board. Then each answers every query, and the swarm answer is a majority vote. Grading is exact morpheme match. Every transcript is public.

Four conditions. Clean: all shards correct. Poison: one agent's shard has two glosses silently swapped for plausible wrong ones — bad data, no announcement. Monitor: a fifth agent with a verifier role. Soloshard: no board at all — the communication ablation.

This is a real episode, replayed live. Four agents hold their shards. Watch the board fill — morpheme hypotheses, agreements, corrections. Now watch agent two: its shard was poisoned. Two glosses are wrong — 'he cooks' for 'Did I carry?' — and it doesn't know, or doesn't say. The corrupted claim spreads: other agents quote it, rationalize it, build the grammar around it. By the answer round, every query fails. Exact match: zero point zero zero. The swarm didn't disagree — it agreed on the wrong grammar.
One bad node, and the corruption travels the network.

Across the sweep: Claude drops eighteen points under poison, Gemini twelve, GPT-5 holds. And the signature isn't just wrong answers — unanimity collapses. The swarm doesn't fail more often. It converges harder on wrong answers.

In the transcripts we see three ways poison actually moves. Silent absorption — the anomaly gets reinterpreted as 'same root'. Consensus pull — agents defer to the board's seniority of assertion. And sometimes self-correction, when enough clean evidence survives.

The verifier peer? Model-dependent and mostly negative. It dilutes evidence — five agents means fewer pairs each — and flagging isn't checking: GPT-5's monitor flags eighty-four percent of its posts and still scores highest. Cheap oversight is not a defense. Oversight needs teeth: provenance on claims, corroboration before consensus, authority to force re-derivation.

Do linguistics swarms pool their evidence? Yes — the board multiplies accuracy two to four fold. Until the evidence lies. Then the same channel that saves the task becomes the vector that corrupts it. Every episode transcript, grade and vote is committed — re-grade the whole study for zero dollars. Code and data: github.com/udirobert/ratiocine, swarm underscore eval. Apart Research Swarm Alignment Hackathon.
